episode.title: The Yellow Wallpaper
episode.context: A young woman in the late 1800s is taken to a summer estate by her physician husband to recover from what he calls 'nervous depression.' Confined to a room with strange yellow wallpaper, her mental state begins to unravel as she becomes obsessed with the patterns on the walls.
episode.art_style: Watercolor storybook illustration with muted Victorian tones, visible brushstrokes, atmospheric lighting that shifts from warm to unsettling greens and yellows
episode.narrator_style: intimate, confessional female narrator with increasing urgency as the story progresses

narrator.name: The Narrator
narrator.description: A young woman in her late twenties with delicate features, pale complexion, and dark hair pinned up in a loose Victorian style. She wears simple white cotton nightgowns and day dresses. Her eyes grow more hollow and intense as the story progresses.

john.name: John
john.description: A tall, well-groomed man in his mid-thirties with a neat beard and kind but dismissive eyes. He wears the dark formal attire of a respected physician—waistcoat, watch chain, and crisp white shirts.

nursery.name: The Nursery Room
nursery.description: A large airy room at the top of the house with barred windows, a heavy bed nailed to the floor, and walls covered in torn, faded yellow wallpaper with a chaotic, unsettling pattern. Rings and fixtures dot the walls from its former use as a children's playroom.

wallpaper.name: The Yellow Wallpaper
wallpaper.description: Sickly yellow wallpaper with a sprawling, chaotic pattern of curves and flourishes. In certain lights, a sub-pattern emerges—shapes that seem to move, suggesting bars and a figure trapped behind them. It is torn in patches, particularly around the bed.

estate.name: The Summer Estate
estate.description: A grand colonial mansion set back from the road, surrounded by overgrown gardens with shaded arbors, old hedges, and winding paths. It has an air of faded elegance and abandonment.

sentences: It's not often that ordinary people like my husband John and myself get to rent a grand ancestral estate for the summer.
A colonial mansion with hedges and locked gates—I'd call it a haunted house if I wanted to be romantic about it.
scenes.video_description: A horse-drawn carriage approaches a grand but slightly neglected colonial mansion through iron gates. Overgrown hedges line the drive, and the afternoon light filters through ancient trees.
scenes.camera_style: Wide establishing shot, slowly pushing toward the mansion

sentences: But there is something strange about this place—I can feel it.
Why else would such a beautiful house sit empty for so long, rented out so cheaply?
scenes.video_description: Close-up of the mansion's facade showing cracked paint, dusty windows, and wild roses climbing unchecked. A broken greenhouse sits in the background.
scenes.camera_style: Slow pan across architectural details

sentences: John laughs at me when I say such things, but that's what husbands do.
He's a physician—very practical, very scientific—and he has no patience for things that can't be measured or written down in figures.
scenes.video_description: John helps his wife down from the carriage, smiling indulgently. She looks up at the house with wonder while he checks his pocket watch.
scenes.camera_style: Medium two-shot, focusing on their contrasting expressions

sentences: Here's the thing I can't tell anyone—I'm not getting better.
John says there's nothing really wrong with me except some temporary nervousness, a slight hysterical tendency.
My brother, who is also a doctor, says the same thing.
scenes.video_description: The narrator sits alone in a garden seat, her journal hidden in her lap. She looks tired and pale against the lush green backdrop.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up on her face, soft focus on the garden behind

sentences: But what can you do when a physician of high standing—your own husband—tells everyone you're fine?
I've been prescribed tonics, rest, fresh air, and absolutely forbidden to work until I'm well again.
scenes.video_description: A medicine tray with various bottles sits on a bedside table. The narrator's hand reaches for one reluctantly.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up on the medicine bottles, pull back to show her reluctant expression

sentences: Personally, I disagree with their ideas.
I believe that interesting work and some excitement would do me good.
But they won't hear of it.
scenes.video_description: The narrator attempts to write at a small desk, but hears footsteps and quickly hides her papers. Her face shows frustration.
scenes.camera_style: Over-the-shoulder shot, quick cut to her hiding the journal

sentences: I do write secretly, despite what they say.
It exhausts me, having to be so sneaky about it, but I must say what I feel somehow—it's such a relief.
scenes.video_description: Candlelight illuminates the narrator writing in her journal late at night, glancing nervously at the door.
scenes.camera_style: Intimate close-up, warm candlelight contrasting with shadows

sentences: Let me tell you about this house instead—it really is beautiful.
It stands alone, surrounded by walls and hedges, with the most delicious garden full of shaded paths and grape arbors.
scenes.video_description: Sunlit garden paths wind between overgrown hedges and flowering bushes. Dappled light creates patterns on the ground.
scenes.camera_style: Flowing tracking shot through the garden paths

sentences: Apparently there was some legal trouble over the inheritance, and the place sat empty for years.
That should spoil my ghost story idea, but I don't care—there's something strange here, and I can feel it.
scenes.video_description: The narrator walks alone through the garden, pausing to look back at the mansion. Long shadows stretch across the lawn.
scenes.camera_style: Wide shot with the narrator small against the looming house

sentences: I mentioned this feeling to John one moonlit evening.
He said what I was feeling was a draft, and shut the window.
scenes.video_description: Moonlight streams through a window as John firmly closes it. The narrator sits on the bed looking deflated.
scenes.camera_style: Medium shot, John's back to camera, narrator's disappointed face visible

sentences: I get unreasonably angry with John sometimes.
I never used to be so sensitive—it must be this nervous condition.
But he says if I give in to such feelings, I'll lose my self-control, so I try very hard to hide my frustration.
scenes.video_description: The narrator grips the edge of a chair, composing her face into a pleasant expression as footsteps approach.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up on her hands, then her forced smile

sentences: I don't like our room at all.
I wanted a lovely room downstairs with roses around the window and pretty old-fashioned curtains.
But John wouldn't hear of it.
scenes.video_description: A glimpse of a charming ground-floor room with sunlight and roses at the window, then the door closes on it.
scenes.camera_style: Tracking shot through the doorway, door swinging shut

sentences: Instead, we're in the old nursery at the top of the house.
It's big and airy, with windows on all sides—but those windows have bars on them, from when children lived here.
scenes.video_description: Wide shot of the nursery room showing barred windows, rings on the walls, and the heavy bed. Light streams in but feels trapped.
scenes.camera_style: Slow pan across the room from doorway

sentences: John says we came here just for me, that I need perfect rest and all the air I can breathe.
He's very careful and loving—he takes all the worry from me and schedules every hour of my day.
I feel terribly ungrateful not to appreciate it more.
scenes.video_description: John hands his wife a written schedule while patting her hand reassuringly. She looks at it with tired eyes.
scenes.camera_style: Medium shot focusing on the exchange

sentences: But this wallpaper—I have never seen anything worse in my life.
It's a sprawling, chaotic pattern that commits every artistic sin imaginable.
scenes.video_description: First clear view of the yellow wallpaper, its sickly color and confusing pattern filling the frame. The design seems to twist and writhe.
scenes.camera_style: Slow zoom into the wallpaper pattern

sentences: The pattern is dull enough to confuse the eye, yet pronounced enough to constantly irritate you.
When you try to follow its curves, they suddenly change direction in outrageous angles, destroying themselves in impossible contradictions.
scenes.video_description: Abstract animation of the wallpaper pattern, curves leading nowhere, angles that make no logical sense.
scenes.camera_style: Tight close-up, slowly moving across the pattern

sentences: And the color—it's repulsive.
A smoldering, unclean yellow, strangely faded by the sunlight.
In some places it's a dull orange, in others a sickly sulfur tint.
scenes.video_description: Different sections of the wallpaper showing its varied, unpleasant yellows in changing light conditions.
scenes.camera_style: Series of close-ups with shifting light

sentences: The paper is torn off in patches all around the head of my bed, as far as I can reach.
The children who lived here before must have hated it too.
scenes.video_description: Torn patches of wallpaper around the bed frame, revealing bare plaster underneath. The narrator's hand traces the edge of one tear.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up on the torn sections, hand entering frame

sentences: John is away most of the day, and sometimes at night when his patients need him.
I'm glad my case isn't serious—at least that's what he tells me.
scenes.video_description: John leaves through the front door with his medical bag while the narrator watches from an upstairs window.
scenes.camera_style: Shot from inside, through the barred window, watching him leave

sentences: But these nervous troubles are dreadfully depressing.
John doesn't know how much I really suffer—he knows there's no reason for me to suffer, and that satisfies him.
scenes.video_description: The narrator lies on the bed, staring at the ceiling, tears silently rolling down her cheeks.
scenes.camera_style: Overhead shot looking down at her on the bed

sentences: It weighs on me terribly that I can't do my duty.
I meant to be such a help to John, such a comfort.
And here I am, already a burden.
scenes.video_description: The narrator attempts simple household tasks but has to stop, exhausted. She sinks into a chair, defeated.
scenes.camera_style: Following shot showing her struggle and collapse

sentences: It's fortunate that Mary is so good with the baby.
Such a dear little thing—but I cannot be with him.
He makes me too nervous.
scenes.video_description: Through a doorway, we glimpse a nursemaid holding a baby. The narrator watches from a distance, longing but unable to approach.
scenes.camera_style: POV shot through a partially open door, soft focus

sentences: John laughs at me about this wallpaper.
At first he meant to have it replaced, but then he said I was letting it get the better of me.
scenes.video_description: John gestures dismissively at the wallpaper while the narrator looks at him pleadingly.
scenes.camera_style: Two-shot showing their different reactions to the walls

sentences: He said that giving in to such fancies is the worst thing for a nervous patient.
If he changed the wallpaper, I'd next want to change the bed, then the windows, then everything else.
scenes.video_description: Quick cuts showing the heavy bed, the barred windows, the gate at the stairs—all feeling increasingly like a prison.
scenes.camera_style: Rapid montage of confining elements

sentences: When I asked if we could move downstairs to one of the pretty rooms, he took me in his arms and called me a blessed little goose.
He said he'd go live in the cellar if I wanted, just to make fun of me.
scenes.video_description: John embraces his wife patronizingly while she looks small and frustrated in his arms.
scenes.camera_style: Medium shot emphasizing the size difference and her trapped expression

sentences: But I suppose he's right about the room.
It is airy and comfortable enough.
I would be silly to make him uncomfortable over a whim.
scenes.video_description: The narrator sits by a window, forcing herself to look content. Sunlight illuminates her face but her eyes are empty.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up with harsh window light creating shadows

sentences: From one window I can see the garden with its mysterious shaded paths.
From another, I see the bay and a little private wharf.
Sometimes I fancy I see people walking among the arbors, but John says I must not give way to such imaginings.
scenes.video_description: Beautiful views from the windows—garden paths, distant water, arbors in shadow. Fleeting shapes seem to move among the trees.
scenes.camera_style: POV shots through different windows, glimpses of movement

sentences: He says that with my imaginative nature and habit of making up stories, my nervousness will lead me to all sorts of excited fancies.
I ought to use my willpower to check these tendencies.
So I try.
scenes.video_description: The narrator forces herself to look away from the window, closing her eyes and pressing her hands to her temples.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up on her face showing internal struggle

sentences: I think sometimes that if I were well enough to write, it would relieve the pressure of all these ideas inside me.
But I get so tired when I try.
scenes.video_description: The narrator stares at a blank page, pen in hand, but her hand trembles and she sets it down.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up on the blank page and her trembling hand

sentences: It's so discouraging to have no one to talk to about my thoughts.
John says when I'm really better, we can invite my cousins to visit—but not now.
He says stimulating company would be like putting fireworks in my pillow.
scenes.video_description: An empty sitting room with two chairs facing each other—one occupied by the narrator, the other empty and waiting.
scenes.camera_style: Wide shot emphasizing the empty chair and her loneliness

sentences: I wish I could get well faster.
But I must not think about that—thinking about my condition always makes me feel worse.
scenes.video_description: The narrator paces the room slowly, her reflection caught in a dusty mirror showing a pale, anxious face.
scenes.camera_style: Tracking shot following her movement, catching the mirror reflection

sentences: This paper seems to know what a terrible influence it has.
There's a spot where the pattern looks like a broken neck with two bulging eyes staring down at you.
scenes.video_description: The wallpaper pattern resolves momentarily into a disturbing face-like image before dissolving back into abstract shapes.
scenes.camera_style: Slow zoom revealing the face in the pattern

sentences: I get positively angry with its boldness.
Those unblinking eyes crawl up and down and sideways across the walls—they're everywhere.
scenes.video_description: Multiple eye-like shapes in the wallpaper pattern seem to follow the viewer as the camera pans across the room.
scenes.camera_style: Paranoid tracking shot, eyes seeming to move

sentences: I never saw so much expression in an inanimate thing before.
As a child, I used to lie awake finding faces in blank walls and making friends of furniture.
I suppose that imaginative nature is still with me.
scenes.video_description: Childhood memory sequence—a young girl in bed, finding comfort in the wink of brass doorknobs and the friendly shape of an old chair.
scenes.camera_style: Soft, nostalgic lighting, dreamy transitions

sentences: The children who used this room before me must have been wild things.
The floor is scratched and gouged, the plaster dug out in places.
The heavy bed looks as if it survived a war.
scenes.video_description: Details of damage throughout the room—scratches on floorboards, holes in plaster, the battered bed frame bolted to the floor.
scenes.camera_style: Series of detail shots showing wear and damage

sentences: But I don't mind any of that—only the paper bothers me.
John's sister Jennie is here now, taking care of the house.
She's a perfect housekeeper, and I think she believes the writing made me sick.
scenes.video_description: Jennie, a capable-looking woman, bustles through the house with linens. The narrator quickly hides her journal when she approaches.
scenes.camera_style: Quick cut from normal activity to concealment

sentences: But I can write when she's out.
From these windows I can see her coming from a long way off—the road winds beautifully through the countryside.
scenes.video_description: The narrator writes quickly by the window, glancing up periodically to watch the distant road through the trees.
scenes.camera_style: Split focus—close on writing, background showing the view

sentences: This wallpaper has a kind of second pattern, a shadow pattern that you can only see in certain lights.
Where the sun hits it just right, there's a strange, provoking shape that seems to lurk behind the main design.
scenes.video_description: Sunlight shifts across the wallpaper, and for a moment a secondary pattern emerges—formless but somehow humanoid, lurking behind the foreground design.
scenes.camera_style: Time-lapse of light changing, revealing hidden pattern

sentences: The Fourth of July has come and gone.
John thought visitors might do me good, so we had family down for a week.
I didn't do a thing—Jennie handled everything—but it exhausted me all the same.
scenes.video_description: Glimpses of a family gathering—children playing on the lawn, adults in the parlor—while the narrator watches from a window above, separated.
scenes.camera_style: High angle shot from the nursery window looking down

sentences: John says if I don't improve faster, he'll send me to a famous nerve specialist in the fall.
A friend of mine went to him once—she says he's just like John and my brother, only worse.
I don't want to go there at all.
scenes.video_description: The narrator imagines a cold clinical office, a stern doctor's face, instruments and restraints. She shudders and returns to reality.
scenes.camera_style: Brief nightmare sequence, harsh lighting, then return to normal

sentences: I don't feel like anything is worth the effort anymore.
I cry at nothing, and cry most of the time.
But never when John is here—only when I'm alone.
scenes.video_description: The narrator sits in sunlight but weeps silently. At the sound of footsteps, she quickly wipes her face and arranges a smile.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up on tears, quick transition to composed face

sentences: I'm alone quite a lot now.
John is often kept in town, and Jennie is good about leaving me in peace.
So I walk in the garden, sit on the porch, and lie up here in this room a great deal.
scenes.video_description: Montage of solitary activities—slow walks through overgrown paths, sitting alone on the porch, lying on the bed staring at the ceiling.
scenes.camera_style: Series of melancholy shots, each more isolated than the last

sentences: I'm getting fond of this room, in spite of the wallpaper.
Perhaps because of the wallpaper.
It occupies my mind completely.
scenes.video_description: The narrator lies on the bed, her eyes fixed on the wallpaper with an intensity that borders on obsession.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up of her eyes, then what she sees—the pattern consuming her vision

sentences: I lie here on this immovable bed—it's nailed to the floor, you know—and I follow that pattern for hours.
It's like exercise for my mind, trying to find some order in the chaos.
scenes.video_description: The camera becomes the narrator's eyes, moving across the wallpaper pattern, trying to find logic in its madness.
scenes.camera_style: POV tracking shot across the wallpaper

sentences: I know something about design, and this pattern follows no rules whatsoever.
No law of symmetry, no rhythm, no repetition that makes sense.
It is chaos pretending to be order.
scenes.video_description: Animated diagram attempting to map the wallpaper's logic, lines and measurements that lead nowhere and contradict themselves.
scenes.camera_style: Abstract analytical view of the pattern

sentences: The pattern runs horizontally and vertically and diagonally—all at once.
You think you've mastered it, and then it does a somersault and leaves you lost again.
It's like a bad dream.
scenes.video_description: The wallpaper seems to shift and move, patterns running in impossible directions simultaneously, disorienting and dizzying.
scenes.camera_style: Surreal animation of shifting pattern

sentences: The outside pattern reminds me of fungus—toadstools budding and sprouting in endless twisted shapes.
It makes me tired just to look at it.
scenes.video_description: The pattern transforms into organic fungal imagery—mushrooms sprouting and spreading in accelerated growth.
scenes.camera_style: Morphing transition from wallpaper to fungi

sentences: I don't know why I keep writing about this—I don't want to.
But I must express what I feel somehow.
The effort is becoming greater than the relief.
scenes.video_description: The narrator's handwriting in her journal grows more erratic, the pages filling with obsessive descriptions of patterns.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up on deteriorating handwriting

sentences: John says I must eat more and take my medicines and sleep all I can.
Dear John—he loves me very much and hates to see me sick.
scenes.video_description: John sits beside the bed reading to his wife while she lies listlessly. His face shows concern but also frustration.
scenes.camera_style: Soft lighting, intimate domestic scene with underlying tension

sentences: I tried to have a real conversation with him the other day—to tell him how I wish I could visit my cousins.
But he said I wasn't strong enough to go, and I started crying before I could finish explaining.
I can't seem to think straight anymore.
scenes.video_description: The narrator tries to speak but dissolves into tears. John carries her to bed like a child, looking helpless.
scenes.camera_style: Emotional sequence, close-ups on both faces

sentences: He gathered me up in his arms and told me I was his darling, his comfort, all he had.
He says only I can help myself—that I must use my willpower and not let silly fancies run away with me.
scenes.video_description: John holds his wife close, but the embrace looks more like containment than comfort. Her eyes are fixed on the wallpaper over his shoulder.
scenes.camera_style: Over-shoulder shot showing her gaze fixed on the wall

sentences: There's one comfort—our baby is well and happy, and doesn't have to sleep in this horrible room.
What a lucky escape for that dear child.
I would never let an impressionable little thing live in a room like this.
scenes.video_description: A glimpse of the baby sleeping peacefully in a sunny, normal nursery elsewhere in the house—stark contrast to the yellow room.
scenes.camera_style: Warm, safe lighting, then cut back to the ominous nursery

sentences: I never mention the wallpaper to them anymore—I'm too wise for that now.
But I keep watch over it.
There are things in that paper that nobody knows but me, and nobody ever will.
scenes.video_description: The narrator's face takes on a secretive, knowing expression. Her eyes move across the wallpaper with new purpose.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up showing transformation in her demeanor

sentences: Behind the front pattern, the dim shapes are getting clearer every day.
It's always the same shape—repeated countless times across the walls.
And it's like a woman, stooping down and creeping behind the pattern.
scenes.video_description: The secondary pattern resolves into a crouching female figure, repeated endlessly behind the bars of the primary design.
scenes.camera_style: Slow reveal of the woman shape in the pattern

sentences: I don't like it at all.
I wonder... I begin to think... I wish John would take me away from here.
scenes.video_description: The narrator presses her back against the opposite wall, staring at the wallpaper with growing fear. The figure seems to shift.
scenes.camera_style: Wide shot showing her trapped between walls

sentences: It's so hard to talk to John about my condition.
He's so wise, and he loves me so much.
But I tried again last night, in the moonlight.
scenes.video_description: Moonlight fills the room with silver light. The narrator lies awake while John sleeps, watching the shadows on the wall.
scenes.camera_style: Blue-silver moonlit atmosphere, intimate and tense

sentences: I hate to see moonlight on that wallpaper—it creeps in so slowly.
The faint figure behind the pattern seemed to shake it, as if she was trying to get out.
scenes.video_description: Moonlight creeps across the wallpaper. The woman-shape behind the pattern seems to move, pushing against the bars of the design.
scenes.camera_style: Slow tracking shot following moonlight, pattern stirring

sentences: I got up quietly and went to touch the paper, to see if it really moved.
When I came back to bed, John was awake.
He asked what his 'little girl' was doing wandering about.
scenes.video_description: The narrator's hand reaches toward the wallpaper in the darkness. She jerks back at John's voice.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up on hand approaching wall, quick cut to startled face

sentences: I told him I wasn't really getting better here, and I wanted to leave.
He said our lease is up in three weeks, and he can't possibly leave town now.
Besides, he says I am getting better—gaining weight and color—whether I can see it or not.
scenes.video_description: John sits up in bed, speaking reasonably while the narrator looks increasingly desperate.
scenes.camera_style: Shot-reverse-shot showing their disconnect

sentences: I said I don't weigh any more, not really, and my appetite is only better when he's here.
He hugged me and called me his 'little heart' and said we should sleep and talk in the morning.
As if morning would change anything.
scenes.video_description: John pulls her close dismissively. Her eyes stay open, staring at the wall over his shoulder in the darkness.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up on her eyes, wallpaper reflected in them

sentences: I started to say that I felt better in body perhaps, but not in mind...
He cut me off with such a stern look that I couldn't say another word.
scenes.video_description: John's face hardens into a stern expression. The narrator visibly shrinks back.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up on his stern face, then her retreat

sentences: He begged me, for his sake and our child's, never to let such ideas enter my mind again.
He called it a false and foolish fancy.
He asked if I couldn't trust him as my physician.
scenes.video_description: John speaks earnestly, gripping her shoulders. The wallpaper looms behind them both, the woman-shape seeming to watch.
scenes.camera_style: Medium shot with wallpaper prominently in background

sentences: So I said nothing more, and we went to sleep.
Or he did.
I lay awake for hours, trying to decide whether the front pattern and the back pattern really move together, or separately.
scenes.video_description: The room in darkness. John sleeps peacefully while the narrator stares at the ceiling, her mind clearly elsewhere.
scenes.camera_style: High angle shot of both in bed, she alone in wakefulness

sentences: In daylight, the pattern's chaos is maddening to a normal mind.
You think you've understood it, and then it turns on you—slaps you down, tramples you.
It's like being trapped in a nightmare that follows rules you can never learn.
scenes.video_description: Harsh daylight on the wallpaper. The pattern seems aggressive now, overwhelming, filling the entire frame.
scenes.camera_style: Increasingly claustrophobic shots of the pattern

sentences: There's one thing about this paper that nobody notices but me.
It changes as the light changes.
That's why I watch it constantly.
scenes.video_description: Time-lapse of the room as light shifts through the day—the wallpaper transforming subtly with each change.
scenes.camera_style: Time-lapse with focus on the wallpaper's transformations

sentences: By moonlight, I wouldn't know it was the same paper.
At night, in any light—twilight, candlelight, moonlight—the outer pattern becomes bars.
And the woman behind them is as plain as day.
scenes.video_description: The wallpaper pattern transforms in dim light—the curves becoming prison bars, the woman-shape pressing against them desperately.
scenes.camera_style: Dramatic shift from day to night appearance

sentences: I didn't realize for the longest time what I was seeing behind that pattern.
But now I'm certain—it's a woman.
In daylight, she stays quiet, kept still by the pattern.
scenes.video_description: The woman-shape in full detail—a crouching female figure, frozen in the pattern during daylight, watching.
scenes.camera_style: Slow reveal of the complete figure

sentences: I lie down so much now.
John says it's good for me, and he started the habit by making me rest after every meal.
But I don't actually sleep—I watch.
scenes.video_description: The narrator lies on the bed, perfectly still, eyes wide open, watching the walls with predatory attention.
scenes.camera_style: Low angle shot from beside the bed, her watchful eyes

sentences: This has taught me to be deceitful.
I don't tell them I'm awake.
I don't tell them what I see.
scenes.video_description: John and Jennie peek in the door. The narrator appears to sleep peacefully. The moment they leave, her eyes snap open.
scenes.camera_style: Shot through doorway, then close-up on opening eyes

sentences: The fact is, I'm getting a little afraid of John.
He seems strange sometimes.
And Jennie has an odd look about her too.
scenes.video_description: John and Jennie exchange worried glances when they think the narrator isn't looking. She watches them from a mirror.
scenes.camera_style: Caught in reflection, suspicious looks all around

sentences: It occurs to me, just as a hypothesis, that perhaps the paper is affecting them too.
I've caught John looking at the wallpaper.
I've caught Jennie with her hand on it.
scenes.video_description: Quick cuts: John staring at the wall with a troubled expression, Jennie touching the paper and jerking her hand back.
scenes.camera_style: Suspenseful quick cuts, each person caught unaware

sentences: When I asked Jennie what she was doing, she turned around as if I'd caught her stealing.
She said the paper stains everything it touches—she'd found yellow marks on our clothes.
But I know she was studying that pattern.
scenes.video_description: Jennie looks guilty and defensive, holding up clothing with yellow stains. The narrator's eyes narrow with suspicion.
scenes.camera_style: Confrontational two-shot, tension between them

sentences: I'm determined that no one will find out about the woman but me.
Life is much more exciting now—I have something to watch for, to look forward to.
I really am eating better.
scenes.video_description: The narrator eats her meal with unusual appetite, a secretive smile on her face, eyes darting to the walls.
scenes.camera_style: Medium shot showing her improved energy, but unsettling affect

sentences: John is pleased to see me improve.
He laughed and said I seemed to be flourishing in spite of the wallpaper.
I didn't tell him it was because of the wallpaper.
scenes.video_description: John chuckles and pats her hand approvingly. She smiles back, hiding her true thoughts.
scenes.camera_style: Ironic contrast between his relief and her secret knowledge

sentences: I don't want to leave now until I've figured it out.
There's a week left, and I think that will be enough time.
I'm feeling ever so much better—though I don't sleep much at night anymore.
scenes.video_description: Calendar pages flutter—one week remains. The narrator studies the wallpaper with scholarly intensity.
scenes.camera_style: Time-lapse of days passing, she grows more absorbed

sentences: I sleep during the day when the pattern is tiresome and confusing.
But at night, when it changes and the woman moves—that's when I must watch.
scenes.video_description: Day and night cycle rapidly—she sleeps in sunlight, wakes in moonlight, always watching.
scenes.camera_style: Accelerated day-night cycles showing her reversed schedule

sentences: There are always new shoots on the fungus pattern, new shades of that horrible yellow.
And there's something else now—a smell.
It creeps all over the house.
scenes.video_description: Yellow mist seems to emanate from the wallpaper, drifting through the house, under doors, down stairs.
scenes.camera_style: Tracking shot following the spreading yellow vapor

sentences: I find it hiding in the dining room, lurking in the parlor, lying in wait on the stairs.
It gets into my hair.
I can smell it even when I leave the house—I turn my head quickly and there it is.
scenes.video_description: The narrator sniffs the air with increasing paranoia throughout the house. Even outside, she whips her head around as if pursued.
scenes.camera_style: Jarring POV shots, constant vigilance

sentences: I once thought about burning the house down just to destroy that smell.
But I'm used to it now.
The only thing I can compare it to is the color of the paper itself—a yellow smell.
scenes.video_description: Flames reflected in the narrator's eyes for a moment, then gone. She breathes in the yellow air as if it's normal now.
scenes.camera_style: Disturbing close-up, brief fire imagery, then resignation

sentences: There's a very strange mark on the wall, down low near the floor.
A long streak that runs all the way around the room, as if something had been rubbed against it over and over.
Round and round and round.
scenes.video_description: A worn groove running along the baseboard all around the room, worn smooth by repeated contact.
scenes.camera_style: Low tracking shot following the mark around the room

sentences: I have finally discovered something.
By watching at night when the pattern changes, I've figured it out.
The front pattern moves—and no wonder. The woman behind it is shaking it.
scenes.video_description: Night. The wallpaper pattern visibly trembles as the woman-shape pushes against it from behind, desperate to escape.
scenes.camera_style: Dramatic reveal, pattern shaking violently

sentences: Sometimes I think there are many women behind the pattern, and sometimes only one.
She crawls around fast, and her crawling shakes everything.
In the bright spots she freezes. In the shadows she grabs the bars and shakes them hard.
scenes.video_description: Multiple women-shapes appear and merge, crawling behind the bars. They freeze in light, shake the pattern in shadow.
scenes.camera_style: Surreal animation of multiplying, moving figures

sentences: She's always trying to climb through.
But nobody could climb through that pattern—it strangles them.
That's why it has so many heads—they get through and the pattern chokes them off.
scenes.video_description: Horrific image: heads emerging through the wallpaper pattern, being twisted, going still. Eyes turned white.
scenes.camera_style: Slow horror reveal, building dread

sentences: I think that woman gets out during the day.
I've seen her—creeping in the lane, in the garden, under the trees.
She's always creeping.
scenes.video_description: Distant figure of a woman crawling through the garden, under trees, along the road. Always creeping, never standing.
scenes.camera_style: Distant shots of the creeping figure in various locations

sentences: I see her out of every window.
When a carriage comes, she hides under the blackberry vines.
I don't blame her—it must be humiliating to be caught creeping by daylight.
scenes.video_description: Multiple windows showing the same creeping woman, ducking behind vines as a carriage passes.
scenes.camera_style: Multi-panel showing different windows, same figure

sentences: I always lock the door when I creep by daylight.
I can't do it at night—John would suspect something.
But during the day, when I'm alone, I creep.
scenes.video_description: The narrator on her hands and knees, crawling along the baseboard of the room, her shoulder against the wall, fitting into that worn groove.
scenes.camera_style: Shocking reveal of her creeping, matter-of-fact

sentences: And John is acting so strange lately—I don't want to irritate him.
I wish he would sleep in another room.
I don't want anyone else to get that woman out at night—only me.
scenes.video_description: The narrator watches John sleep, her eyes calculating. Then she turns to watch the wallpaper, possessive.
scenes.camera_style: Unsettling shot of her watching both her husband and the wall

sentences: I often wonder if I could see her out of all the windows at once.
But no matter how fast I turn, I can only see out of one at a time.
And though I always see her, she might be able to creep faster than I can turn.
scenes.video_description: The narrator spins between windows, trying to catch the figure from multiple angles. Always one step behind.
scenes.camera_style: Dizzying spinning shot between windows

sentences: If only I could get that top pattern off the under one!
I mean to try it, little by little.
I've found something else too—but I won't tell. It doesn't do to trust people too much.
scenes.video_description: The narrator's fingernails picking at the edge of the wallpaper, peeling a small corner. A secretive smile on her face.
scenes.camera_style: Close-up on her fingers working at the paper

sentences: There are only two days left to get this paper off.
I think John is starting to notice something.
I don't like the look in his eyes.
scenes.video_description: John asks professional questions, examining his wife with clinical concern. She avoids his gaze.
scenes.camera_style: Tense two-shot, suspicion on both sides

sentences: He asked Jennie lots of questions about me.
She gave a good report—she said I sleep a great deal during the day.
John knows I don't sleep well at night, no matter how quiet I am.
scenes.video_description: Through a doorway, John and Jennie confer quietly. The narrator watches from the shadows.
scenes.camera_style: Eavesdropping shot through crack in door

sentences: Hurrah! This is the last day, and it's enough.
John has to stay in town overnight and won't be back until evening.
Jennie wanted to sleep in my room, but I told her I'd rest better alone.
scenes.video_description: John departs in a carriage. Jennie offers to stay with the narrator, who smiles and declines sweetly.
scenes.camera_style: Watch them leave, then the smile becomes something else

sentences: That was clever of me—because I wasn't alone at all.
As soon as the moonlight came, and that poor thing began to crawl and shake the pattern, I got up to help her.
I pulled and she shook, I shook and she pulled.
scenes.video_description: Moonlight floods the room. The narrator rises and begins tearing at the wallpaper in a frenzy, working with the figure behind it.
scenes.camera_style: Dynamic shots of tearing, moonlit destruction

sentences: Before morning, we had peeled off yards of that paper.
A strip as high as my head, halfway around the room.
And when the sun came and that awful pattern began to laugh at me, I declared I would finish it today.
scenes.video_description: Dawn light reveals devastation—great swaths of wallpaper torn away, the narrator wild-eyed and determined.
scenes.camera_style: Wide shot showing the destruction and her resolution

sentences: We leave tomorrow, and they're moving all the furniture back downstairs.
Jennie looked at the wall in amazement, but I told her cheerfully that I did it out of spite—because I hated that vicious paper.
She laughed, but I saw how she betrayed herself.
scenes.video_description: Jennie stares at the stripped walls in shock. The narrator speaks brightly, watching Jennie's reaction with knowing eyes.
scenes.camera_style: Shot of Jennie's horror, then the narrator's false brightness

sentences: But I am here, and no living person touches this paper but me.
Jennie tried to get me out of the room—it was obvious what she wanted.
But I told her I would lie down and sleep, and not to wake me even for dinner.
scenes.video_description: The narrator firmly closes the door on Jennie, then turns back to face the remaining wallpaper with purpose.
scenes.camera_style: Door closing, then determined turn to face the wall

sentences: So now she's gone, and the servants are gone, and everything has been taken away.
Nothing is left but this great bed nailed to the floor.
I quite enjoy the room now that it's bare.
scenes.video_description: Empty room with only the bed. Torn wallpaper hangs in strips. The narrator surveys her domain with satisfaction.
scenes.camera_style: Slow pan of the empty, damaged room

sentences: I've locked the door and thrown the key out the window into the garden.
I don't want to go out, and I don't want anyone coming in.
Not until John arrives. I want to astonish him.
scenes.video_description: The key arcs through the air, landing in the garden below. The narrator watches it fall with a strange smile.
scenes.camera_style: Tracking shot of the falling key, then her expression

sentences: I have a rope up here that even Jennie didn't find.
If that woman gets out and tries to escape, I can tie her.
But I forgot—I can't reach very far without something to stand on.
scenes.video_description: A rope coiled in the corner. The narrator looks at it, then at the barred windows, then at the immovable bed.
scenes.camera_style: Series of shots: rope, bars, bed—the pieces of her plan

sentences: This bed will not move!
I tried to push it and lift it until I couldn't anymore.
I got so angry I bit off a piece of it—but that hurt my teeth.
scenes.video_description: The narrator struggles with the massive bed, pushing, pulling. In frustration, she bites the wooden frame.
scenes.camera_style: Physical struggle shown, building to the bite

sentences: Then I peeled off all the paper I could reach standing on the floor.
It sticks horribly, and the pattern just seems to enjoy it!
All those strangled heads and bulging eyes shriek with laughter at me.
scenes.video_description: The narrator tears at the wallpaper frantically. The remaining pattern seems to mock her, faces twisted in malicious amusement.
scenes.camera_style: Frenzied tearing intercut with leering pattern faces

sentences: I'm getting angry enough to do something desperate.
Jumping out the window would be good exercise—but the bars are too strong.
Besides, I wouldn't do that. Such a thing would be improper and might be misunderstood.
scenes.video_description: The narrator looks at the barred window, tests the bars. Shakes her head rationally, turns away.
scenes.camera_style: Her considering the window, then dismissing the idea

sentences: I don't like to look out the windows anymore.
There are so many of those creeping women out there, and they creep so fast.
I wonder if they all came out of that wallpaper, as I did.
scenes.video_description: Through the window: dozens of creeping women, moving through the garden, the lane, everywhere. All crawling.
scenes.camera_style: Horrifying wide shot of the creeping multitude

sentences: But I am securely tied now by my well-hidden rope—you won't catch me out on that road.
I suppose I'll have to get back behind the pattern when night comes, and that will be hard.
It's so pleasant to be out in this room and creep around as I please.
scenes.video_description: The narrator creeping along the baseboard, her shoulder in the groove, content. The rope trails from somewhere unseen.
scenes.camera_style: Low angle following her circular path

sentences: I don't want to go outside.
Outside, you have to creep on the ground, and everything is green instead of yellow.
But here I can creep smoothly on the floor, and my shoulder fits perfectly in that long groove around the wall.
scenes.video_description: Her shoulder fits exactly into the worn track. She creeps round and round, peaceful, certain.
scenes.camera_style: Detailed shot of her fitting into the groove

sentences: Why, there's John at the door!
It's no use, young man—you can't open it.
How he does call and pound!
scenes.video_description: Pounding on the locked door. John's muffled voice calling her name. The narrator continues creeping, unconcerned.
scenes.camera_style: Split focus: rattling door, narrator creeping calmly

sentences: Now he's calling for an axe.
It would be a shame to break down such a beautiful door.
I called to him in my gentlest voice—the key is down by the front steps, under a leaf.
scenes.video_description: The narrator speaks sweetly toward the door, still creeping, as John's voice grows more frantic.
scenes.camera_style: Her serene voice contrasted with his panic

sentences: That silenced him for a few moments.
Then he said very quietly, 'Open the door, my darling.'
I can't, I told him—the key is down by the front door, under a leaf.
scenes.video_description: Silence. Then John's quiet, controlled voice. The narrator keeps creeping, repeating herself calmly.
scenes.camera_style: Tension building through the closed door

sentences: I said it several times, very gently, until he had to go and see for himself.
He got it, of course, and came in.
He stopped short by the door.
scenes.video_description: The door opens. John stands frozen in the doorway, seeing the devastated room and his wife creeping along the wall.
scenes.camera_style: His POV of the nightmare scene, then his shocked face

sentences: 'What is the matter?' he cried. 'For God's sake, what are you doing?'
I kept on creeping, but I looked at him over my shoulder.
scenes.video_description: The narrator continues her circular path, turning her head to look at him while she creeps. Her expression is triumphant.
scenes.camera_style: Over-the-shoulder look, unsettling and deliberate

sentences: 'I've got out at last,' I said. 'In spite of you and Jennie.'
'And I've pulled off most of the paper, so you can't put me back.'
scenes.video_description: Close-up on her face—liberated, certain, beyond reason. The torn wallpaper frames her like a broken cage.
scenes.camera_style: Powerful close-up, her transformation complete

sentences: Now why should that man have fainted?
But he did, and right across my path by the wall.
So I had to creep over him every time.
scenes.video_description: John collapses in the doorway. The narrator keeps creeping her endless circuit, climbing over his unconscious body each time she passes.
scenes.camera_style: Final haunting image—her circular path, his fallen form

sentences: And so she continues, round and round, in the room that became her prison and her liberation.
A woman who was told she was not sick, told to rest, told not to write, told not to think.
Until thinking was all she had left.
scenes.video_description: Pull back slowly through the window, the barred window, showing the room growing smaller—the creeping figure still visible within.
scenes.camera_style: Slow retreat through the barred window

sentences: This is the story Charlotte Perkins Gilman wrote in 1892, after her own experience with the 'rest cure.'
She was told by the famous doctor never to write again—never to do any work that engaged her mind.
She nearly went mad.
scenes.video_description: Transition to sepia-toned historical imagery: a woman's writing desk, medical advertisements from the era, a portrait of Gilman.
scenes.camera_style: Documentary-style montage

sentences: Instead, she ignored the advice.
She went back to work, and she wrote.
This story was her answer to those who thought women were too fragile for their own thoughts.
scenes.video_description: Gilman writing at her desk, determined. Pages filled with words. The yellow wallpaper pattern dissolves into flowing script.
scenes.camera_style: Empowering final imagery of creative defiance

sentences: The Yellow Wallpaper by Charlotte Perkins Gilman.
Adapted for this telling from the original 1892 story.
scenes.video_description: Title card with the story title and author, the yellow wallpaper pattern fading to clean white behind elegant text.
scenes.camera_style: Simple title card, dignified ending
